brief.market_summary: US stocks posted a mixed Friday. The S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,561.67 and still rose 2.5% on the week, ending a four-week losing streak. Under the surface, money is rotating hard: semis (SMH) fell 2.99% and tech (XLK) 2.01%, while staples, financials and energy all gained. October PPI came in mostly as expected, but Fed officials kept talking up hikes, and the 10-year Treasury yield rose 5.1bp on the day to 5.154%, up 29.5bp on the week. The dollar index is at a 19-month high of 103.41. Brent was flat at $95.84 for a second weekly loss as the IEA flagged a supply surplus. Crypto took the worst of the rate repricing: by Saturday afternoon (UTC) BTC was at $65,446, its lowest since August and down 13.6% on the week. Other tokens fell 7–9% on the day as $1.47B of leveraged positions were liquidated.
brief.since_last:
- **October PPI (Fri):** headline +0.3% m/m vs +0.4% expected; core +0.3%, in line. On the year, headline rose to 6.5%, the highest since Nov 2022.
- **Fed:** Collins, Jefferson and Daly all leaned toward hikes. A 25bp December hike is priced at about 89% (LSEG), and the hawks are now signalling hikes into 2027 (n144).
- **Rates:** the 10-year closed at 5.154% and the 30-year at 5.481%. October's budget deficit was a record $404B vs $298.6B expected.
- **Semis:** SMH fell another 3% to $486.75, further below the $500 re-entry line. Nvidia fell 2%; HSBC cut it to Hold and lowered its target to $170 from $365.
- **Cisco:** fell 6% despite raising guidance, because orders missed.
- **Crypto:** BTC broke support at $68K and $66K over the weekend. ETH fell below $2,000 and is at $1,831, which almost certainly triggered last brief's ETH trim backstop.
- **Anthropic IPO:** terms are now known. Pricing is Wed 18 Nov at $70–78 a share (about a $1.2T valuation), with Nasdaq trading as "ANT" from Thu 19 Nov.
- **Oil:** Brent was unchanged on the day. The IEA's surplus call, OPEC's October output jump of 1.96M bpd and a 4.66M bbl US crude build outweighed Hormuz headlines.

**Data caveat:** the supplied calendar appears to stamp releases one day late (PPI is shown as 14 Nov; CNBC confirms it came out Fri 13 Nov). It also lists no events next week, while CNBC and Newsquawk show a full slate. I have relied on the dated sources. Applied Materials' results, Cisco's quarterly EPS and the dates of next week's coupon auctions weren't available.

The Nasdaq fell 0.91%, SMH dropped 2.99% and XLK 2.01%, while staples (+1.42%), energy (+0.98%) and financials (+0.81%) gained. Nvidia's leadership crisis (n13, n39) and a 5.15% 10-year are pushing money out of long-duration AI names and into cash-generative defensives ahead of Nvidia on Tuesday and the Anthropic IPO on Thursday.

sections.summary: Treasuries sold off again, led by the middle of the curve. Over the week the 5-year rose 33.3bp to 4.981% and the 10-year 29.5bp to 5.154%, while the 30-year gained only 22.1bp to 5.481%. Fed speakers pushed hikes into 2027 (n144) and October's deficit was a record $404B. Bills are the one part of the curve paying you to wait: the 3-month is at 4.32% par and the 13-week at a 4.12% discount yield. The drop in IG credit (LQD -1.65% on the week) is duration, not spreads; HYG fell only 0.38%.
key_points: **Fed:** Collins backs 'steady, gradual' hikes (n23); Daly signals a December move (n104); Jefferson says inflation decides (n154). Bessent is pushing back on hiking 'too much' (n62, n162).
**Performance:** TLT -3.10% and IEF -1.98% on the week vs SHY -0.56%. Short duration has been the only safe part of the curve.

sections.summary: Brent settled at $95.84 (+2¢) Friday, down 2.5% on the week and 9.5% over the month, its second weekly loss after a 16% drop the week before. Supply is winning over geopolitics for now. The IEA says the market is back in surplus for the first time since the Iran war began (n138); Iraq is pumping at its highest since 2019 (n82); OPEC output jumped 1.96M bpd in October; and US crude stocks rose 4.66M bbl against an expected draw.
key_points: **Hormuz risk:** the premium hasn't gone. Iran reported explosions on four tankers (not verified), Houthis hit Saudi infrastructure, and Iran is budgeting for zero oil revenue (n159).
**Forecasts:** Barclays keeps $100 for 2026 with upside risk (n61); Citi sees $150 if Hormuz disruption persists (n180). Weekly technical bands sit at $91 bear and $98 bull (n114).
**Energy stocks:** XLE rose 5.42% on the week while Brent fell 2.5%. Equities are pricing durable cash flows, not spot crude.
**Caution:** several EnergyNow headlines in this window (e.g. n163, n164, n177) look like reposted older stories, so I'm not treating them as new information.

brief.instructor_take:
Here's what I think matters this weekend. The market has stopped asking whether the Fed is done and started asking how many more hikes are coming. You can see it in prices: the 10-year is up 29.5bp in a week to 5.15%, the dollar is at a 19-month high, and PPI is running 6.5% on the year. When the discount rate jumps, the assets that get hit first are the ones whose value sits furthest in the future or that pay nothing at all: crypto, semis, gold and long bonds. Assets that pay cash today, like staples, health care and financials, quietly gain. Don't read the S&P's +2.5% week as a calm market; it's two different markets averaging out.

Next week packs every catalyst into four days: retail sales and Nvidia on Tuesday, FOMC minutes and Anthropic's pricing on Wednesday, and the ANT debut and Walmart on Thursday. What the crowd may be missing is that a roughly $1.2T IPO is a supply event. Funds sell other AI and crypto holdings to make room for it. That selling should ease once ANT trades, which makes late next week, not this weekend, the more likely window for a relief bounce.

My positioning is patient: idle cash in bills earning over 4%, finish the ETH trim the rule called for, and no semis until Nvidia has reported and SMH holds above $500. I'm not trying to catch the crypto bottom. Liquidations and whale buying are early signs of exhaustion, but seven days of ETF outflows say the marginal buyer hasn't come back.

What would change my mind: retail sales below the 0.2% consensus plus dovish-leaning minutes that pull the 10-year back under 5%. That combination would be my cue to start adding duration and risk.

top_ideas.title: Hold dry powder in T-bills while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep idle cash in T-bills at ~4.1-4.3% while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.thesis: With a December hike about 89% priced and Fed hawks signalling more into 2027, the front end is the only part of the curve that gains from hikes rather than losing to them. SGOV earns roughly 4.1–4.3% with almost no price risk and holds cash ready for the SMH re-entry rule or a better entry in duration or crypto.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start with the Fed's reaction function. Core PPI at 5.0% y/y, CPI 0.1pt above forecast and Collins, Daly and Jefferson all leaning toward hikes mean short rates are more likely to rise than fall over the next three months. T-bills reprice to each new Fed rate within weeks, so SGOV's yield climbs along with the hikes. Longer bonds do the opposite: TLT lost 3.10% and IEF 1.98% this week while SHY lost only 0.56%. A 5.15% 10-year is tempting, but a record $404B October deficit and 6.5% PPI tell me the term premium can rise further, and you aren't paid enough extra over 4.3% bills to take that risk now. The concept here is the opportunity cost of patience: when cash yields over 4%, waiting is no longer expensive. A less experienced investor often feels they must 'do something' with cash in a sell-off, but here holding cash is a position that earns money. I'd change my mind if retail sales and the minutes push the 10-year back under 5% with the Fed sounding less hawkish; that's when I'd start a ladder into IEF.

top_ideas.sizing: All idle cash plus trim proceeds; 15–25% of the portfolio as a cash reserve is reasonable for this setup.

top_ideas.title: Stay out of semis through Nvidia and ANT
top_ideas.one_liner: No semis until Nvidia reports and SMH holds above $500
top_ideas.thesis: SMH fell another 3% Friday to $486.75 and is down 12.9% over the month. The next four sessions bring Nvidia's first report under an interim CEO and a roughly $1.2T IPO competing for AI dollars. The re-entry rule is still in force: buy back the trimmed amount in two halves only after Nvidia beats and SMH holds above $500.
top_ideas.reasoning: This idea is about not owning a binary event when the setup is against you. First, the evidence: good news isn't being rewarded. Cisco raised guidance and fell 6%; Arm grew revenue 27% and the market shrugged (n113). That tells me positioning is still heavy and investors are using rallies to sell. Second, Nvidia has a governance problem on top of earnings risk: Huang's resignation (n13), HSBC halving its target to $170, and Kress taking her first call as interim CEO. Third, the Anthropic IPO prices Wednesday, and big funds will raise cash for it by selling the AI names they already hold. With the 10-year at 5.15%, long-duration growth also faces a higher discount rate. Why SMH rather than avoiding all tech? Semis carry the most AI capex risk and fell most (-2.99% Friday vs the S&P's -0.4%). I'd be wrong if Nvidia beats the $2.47–2.49 EPS bar, guides above $108.7B and SMH holds above $500 for two closes. In that case I rebuild in halves and accept having missed the first few percent, which is a fair price for skipping the coin-flip.

top_ideas.title: Execute the ETH trim backstop below $2,000
top_ideas.one_liner: ETH closed under $2,000: sell the last third of the trim
top_ideas.thesis: ETH has fallen to $1,831, down 18.2% on the week. It was about $1,930 at 16:00 UTC Friday, so Saturday's 00:00 UTC close was almost certainly below $2,000, which triggers last brief's backstop. Sell the unfilled final third and move the proceeds to SGOV. Keep the core position; don't sell it.
top_ideas.reasoning: I set this rule in advance because I knew it would feel bad to follow, and it does: you're selling about 8% below the trigger, after a $1.31B wave of long liquidations that often marks short-term exhaustion. But the drivers haven't changed. The Fed is hiking, the dollar is at a 19-month high, BTC ETFs have bled $1.91B over seven days, and ETH ETF demand barely registered (+$2.3M). The Ethereum Foundation itself sold 5,000 ETH (n43). Voorhees' $97M purchase (n11) is real buying, but one whale doesn't make a trend. The concept is pre-commitment. A stop rule only protects you if you follow it when price has gapped past it, and the classic beginner mistake is deciding a rule 'doesn't apply' because the move already happened. Why trim ETH rather than BTC? ETH has fallen more than BTC on the day, the week and the month, so it is the weaker asset in this sell-off. What would prove me wrong: a quick reclaim of $2,000 on returning ETF inflows. That's why this is only the last third, and the core stays.

lesson.concept: Asset duration and the discount-rate shock
lesson.explanation: Duration isn't only a bond idea. It measures how far in the future an asset's value lies. A stock priced on profits expected ten years out, or a token with no cash flow at all, behaves like a very long bond: when the discount rate (roughly, the 10-year yield) jumps, its present value falls the most. Companies that pay cash today, like grocers, drug makers and banks, are 'short duration' and hold up, and banks can even benefit from higher rates.
lesson.todays_example: The 10-year rose 29.5bp this week to 5.15%. Over the past month, the long-duration side fell: SMH -12.9%, XLK -10.0%, BTC -19.8%, ETH -23.3% and gold -6.8%, plus TLT -3.1% this week. The short-duration side rose: XLV +6.58%, XLP +6.54%, XLF +6.17% and XLU +5.74%. Same macro shock, opposite results, sorted by how far in the future each asset's payoff sits.
